title: Runtime throughput diagnostics & prefetch heuristics deep dive
summary: Deep technical session to diagnose throughput cliffs observed in Nova's on-prem deployment. Focus areas: continuous batching window behavior, prefetch/kv-cache warm paths, max_num_seqs interactions with token limits and admission control. Agreed to run targeted microbenchmarks and share a prioritized knob playbook.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-07
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 78 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Leah Owens (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood Perf Eng); Maya Ruiz (Nova Head ML), Trevor Lin (Nova Platform), Jordan Park (Nova Security), Priya Shah (Nova SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial): Discussed throughput cliffs seen during steady-state traffic; Suspect interaction between small batch windows, cold KV cache, and aggressive max_num_seqs knob. Action: run microbenchmarks and share playbook.

Topics: continuous batching, kv cache warmup/prefetch, admission control, max_num_seqs, token ceilings, quantization fallbacks, VPC latency.

00:00 Samir: alright uh good afternoon everyone thanks for carving out the time this is Samir from Redwood, we're gonna do a deep dive into throughput diagnostics, um, we had your notes and the graph you sent yesterday, Maya, so thanks for that.
00:22 Maya: yeah thanks, um, appreciate you fitting us in. We started seeing these cliffs after the change to the admission control knobs last week, so want to figure out if it's config or infra.
00:37 Leah: quick agenda — reproduce cliffs locally via a microbenchmark, look at scheduler traces, kv-hit rate timeline, and then propose a small set of knobs to try. Sound okay?
00:48 Trevor: sounds good. Also Jordan wants to make sure nothing we try requires opening new firewall ports for the VPC private deploy.
00:57 Jordan: yeah just the usual SSO/keys we can't relax network egress.
01:05 Diego: noted. As a heads up I'll probably ask for kernel traces and GPU utilization snapshots, but we can do that without changing network.
01:14 Samir: quick clarifying q — the cliffs you sent, are they during peaky loads or steady-state?
01:19 Maya: both, but most visible in steady-state 200 qps with 16 token responses typical. Up until 10am on Tue it was fine then after that it started oscillating.
01:31 Leah: ok, first suspicion is prefetched KV cache evaporation and the scheduler shrinking batch window because it sees fewer queued seqs. That interacts with max_num_seqs — if max_num_seqs is too high relative to slot sizes we can starve packing.
01:46 Priya: when you say "evaporation" do you mean eviction due to memory pressure or TTL-based prefetch failure?
01:51 Leah: could be either; we've seen VPC networking bursts cause slight RPC slowdowns and the prefetch client times out so the cache doesn't warm. Then the scheduler loses its steady stream of sequences to pack and it falls back to smaller windows — more overhead per token.
02:09 Trevor: that matches some of our logs — we have occasional 60-200ms spikes on the internal mgmt plane. Could be NAT gateway hiccups.
02:18 Samir: ok let's go through the knobs. We'll call out the ones we recommend trying first: 1) prefetch retries + timeouts (increase from default 50ms to 200ms), 2) prewarm policy on cold-starts (always run one warmup for top 10 prompt prefixes), 3) reduce max_num_seqs from 256 to 128 for the affected model family, and 4) raise min_batch_window_ms from 6 to 12ms to avoid tiny windows.
02:44 Maya: a couple Qs — won't increasing min_batch_window hurt tail latency for single-user flows?
02:49 Diego: yes small risk for single-user low qps, but your traffic is mostly multi-tenant, 200qps. We can try canary with a subset of routes first.
02:59 Jordan: we also need to ensure KMS calls during prewarm are not blocked, that's security policy.
03:05 Samir: quick aside — quantization fallbacks. We noticed when the runtime falls back from int8 path to fp16 because of sequence length mismatch, latency jumps. Diego, can you describe?
03:16 Diego: sure. When token lengths exceed the compiled kernel's expectation, it can route to a slower fallback kernel. That often correlates with poor packing: if lots of short sequences are bunched with a long one, kernel selection chooses conservative path. The scheduler's sloting can reduce this by grouping like-length seqs (sequence bucketing).
03:34 Maya: ok that sounds like something we could instrument — we do have per-request seq length in our logs.
03:40 Leah: perfect. So our microbenchmark will include varying seq-length distributions: uniform short (8-16 tokens), skewed (95% short, 5% long), and stretched (many 64+ token flows). We'll measure throughput, tail-p99 latency, kv-hit rate, and quant-fallback counts.
03:58 Trevor: what's the easiest way for us to run that without impacting production?
04:02 Samir: we'll provide a JMeter script and a small harness that hits a staging private deployment with identical config, plus a list of sample prompts. No production change.
04:12 Priya: good — SRE will block anything that touches prod.
04:16 Leah: another boolean to watch is admission_control.adaptive_backoff_enable. If it's on and mis-tuned it can drop sequences aggressively under perceived overload. Turning it off for the experiment can confirm if it's helping or hurting.
04:30 Maya: we had that on by default, hmm.
04:33 Diego: common observable: queue length goes to zero, but GPUs show <10% utilization intermittently — classic over-eager admission control.
04:43 Samir: ok moving on to KV cache specifics. Two sub-issues: prefetch miss pattern during short bursts, and cold eviction strategy. We recommend enabling two prefetch attempts with exponential backoff and increasing in-memory kv capacity for the hot-table for 24 hours.
04:58 Trevor: raising in-memory cap — does that require node restart?
05:02 Leah: depends on your deployment. In on-prem we can make it dynamic in many cases, but sometimes you need a rolling restart. We'll document both approaches.
05:10 Jordan: anything here that changes persisted logs or PII handling?
05:14 Samir: no, prefetch and cache config are orthogonal to PII; the data remains encrypted at rest. We'll still verify with security team though.
05:22 Maya: can you explain how max_num_seqs interacts again? We left a previous meeting with it set to 512 and thought more is better.
05:30 Diego: more isn't always better. max_num_seqs caps the number of concurrent sequences per GPU. If it's too high relative to batch-slot steal policy, the scheduler may create very wide windows that include a few long sequences, increasing kernel fallback and per-token cost. Also, very high concurrency can increase contention on KV cache locks leading to higher latencies.
05:50 Trevor: so you suggest lowering it; but won't that limit throughput?
05:54 Leah: net effect can be higher throughput if it improves packing and reduces fallback penalties. The microbenchmark will show this tradeoff.
06:02 Samir: we'll try a small matrix: max_num_seqs in {64,128,256}, min_batch_window_ms in {6,12,24}, and admission_control toggled. That gives us 18 runs per workload shape.
06:18 Maya: fine. How long does each run need to be?
06:22 Diego: 10 minutes to hit steady-state for each, but to be safe 15. So 18 runs x 15 minutes = 4.5 hours per workload shape. We can parallelize across nodes.
06:33 Samir: next, networking. Trevor you mentioned NAT spikes — any chance we can route the prefetch traffic through a private vpc peering to avoid NAT?
06:42 Trevor: maybe, but our current architecture uses a gateway that the control-plane uses, we'd need an infra change. For the test we can move the prefetch client to a colocated host to remove the NAT hop.
06:54 Priya: SRE will help with that for staging.
06:57 Jordan: any security approvals needed?
07:00 Samir: none beyond what you already have for staging.
07:03 Leah: quick comment about eviction policy — please check your ttl and hot-table sizes. We saw one customer set ttl=1h which was too low for their traffic pattern; raising to 6-12h greatly improved hit rates.
07:16 Maya: ours is 2h currently. We'll try 6h for the baseline run.
07:21 Diego: also watch for eager eviction when memory fragments. Node-level memory fragmentation can cause eviction even when nominal memory free looks ok. We'll add a memory fragmentation metric to the dashboard.
07:33 Samir: good point.
07:35 [07:35] TRANSCRIPTION GLITCH: Speaker labeled as Speaker 3 here, content may be wrong.
07:40 Jordan: question from security — does prefetch increase the attack surface?
07:44 Leah: prefetch is internal RPC between control-plane and runtime; it uses mTLS and the same auth tokens. No new external endpoints.
07:51 Jordan: ok thanks.
07:53 Samir: moving toward concrete deliverables. We'll send: 1) a knob playbook (Leah + Diego), 2) JMeter harness and sample prompts (Samir), 3) benchmark spreadsheet template with target charts (Diego). Please run them and upload traces.
08:07 Maya: what's the threshold we should aim for?
08:10 Diego: goal is to restore >95% kv-hit for hot prefixes and p99 token latency below your SLA of 250ms. If we can't get there, we look at dedicated reserved capacity as a fallback.
08:22 Trevor: can you remind us about the dedicated option? We discussed reserved GPU pools last quarter.
08:27 Samir: yes Dedicated gives you pinned pools and reduces noisy neighbor risk; but for on-prem it's heavier lift — we want to try tuning first.
08:35 Maya: sounds good.
08:37 Leah: quick note on observability: include per-token timing, batch-window histogram, quant-fallback counter, and kv-prefetch latency in the logs. We'll provide the exact loglines to enable easy parsing.
08:50 Trevor: that's helpful.
08:53 Samir: ok any other blockers?
08:56 Priya: SRE will need the harness to run in staging and a runbook to abort if GPU temps exceed limits. We'll need the runbook prior to testing.
09:05 Samir: we'll provide a safe-run runbook with thresholds.
09:09 Maya: last Q — can you share examples of previous customers who saw similar cliffs?
09:14 Diego: short example: retail customer had similar pattern; resolution was enabling prefetch retries + reducing max_num_seqs to 128 which increased throughput by 18% and reduced p99 by 30ms. Not identical instance but similar root cause.
09:28 Samir: ok great. Let's capture next steps and action items.
09:32 [09:32] End of main discussion — folks stay on for a quick demo of the harness?
09:35 Samir: we'll drop a short demo recording in the doc.
09:38 Leah: demo notes: how to run the JMeter threads, where to put sample prompts (s3 link), env variables to set, and how to parse the CSV for batch-window and kv-hit.
09:49 Trevor: please include parse script.
09:51 Diego: will do.
09:53 Samir: ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the playbook and schedule the 45-min sync for results.
10:00 Maya: thanks all, appreciate it.
